title: Armed alone is not enough: two Fourth Circuit Garner cases on retreating suspects, and the end of Barnes v. Felix
summary: Two published Fourth Circuit decisions this week are the cleanest teaching pair since Barnes v. Felix came down a year ago. In both, the court denied qualified immunity to an officer who shot a retreating suspect, and in both the anchor was Tennessee v. Garner. Ruffin v. Davis, filed April 29, involved an armed 17-year-old who ran from a Columbia, South Carolina officer during a COVID curfew and was shot as he looked back; a gun on a fleeing suspect, by itself, is not an immediate threat. Byers v. Painter, filed in late April, involved a man in mental health crisis holding a hatchet at his waist and walking away on his parents' property; deadly force against that retreating subject was not justified, over a dissent. On April 27 the Supreme Court denied certiorari in Barnes v. Felix for the second time, leaving Deputy Constable Felix's qualified immunity final. The three cases show the totality framework cutting both ways.
coverage: The episode covered two published Fourth Circuit decisions from late April 2026 and the Supreme Court's April 27 certiorari denial in Barnes v. Felix. It did not report checking the Ninth Circuit, the other federal circuits, or the California courts, so coverage of those courts for this week is not confirmed.

The episode gave no docket numbers, no opinion authors for the Fourth Circuit majorities, and no exact filing date for Byers v. Painter beyond late April 2026. It did not say whether it worked from the full opinions or from summaries.

The source is a machine transcript. The surname in Byers v. Painter also appears as Buyers in the transcript; Byers is used here because it appears more often. The specificity rule the episode calls the post-Smith rule was explained in an earlier episode and is not described in this one.
This brief was rebuilt from the episode originally published on May 9, 2026; it was not re-researched, so verify every citation against the opinion before relying on it.

sections.heading: Supreme Court
sections.note: One certiorari denial, which closes the Barnes v. Felix litigation. The episode treated the denial as the end of a ten-year arc and used it to frame the two Fourth Circuit decisions below.

cases.name: Barnes v. Felix
cases.court: Supreme Court (certiorari denied after the Fifth Circuit's decision on remand)
cases.topic: Second certiorari denial, totality framework, shooting into a moving vehicle
cases.caution: The episode described the denial and the Fifth Circuit's remand decision in summary only, without a docket number or a quotation from the order. Verify the order list and the Fifth Circuit opinion before citing either.
cases.facts: Deputy Constable Roberto Felix fired on a vehicle that was beginning to move while he was hemmed in beside it, next to the door. The Supreme Court's merits decision in Barnes v. Felix, issued about a year before this episode, established the totality framework: an officer's use of force is evaluated against the entire arc of the encounter, not just the moment force was used. On remand, the Fifth Circuit applied that framework and concluded that Felix acted reasonably in firing, so his qualified immunity ruling stood. The case then returned to the Supreme Court on a second petition for certiorari. The episode described the litigation as a ten-year arc, and noted that the Barnes framework has been the backdrop for the circuit decisions it has covered since the merits decision came down.
cases.holding: On April 27, 2026, the Supreme Court denied certiorari in Barnes v. Felix for the second time. That ends the case. Felix's qualified immunity stands, and the Fifth Circuit's ruling on remand, which applied the totality framework and found Felix reasonable in firing on a vehicle that was beginning to move with him hemmed in beside it, is final. The episode's reason for closing the loop was that the same framework produces officer wins on one set of facts and officer losses on another. Felix faced an immediate deadly threat: the vehicle was moving, he was beside the door and hemmed in, and the threat was contemporaneous with the use of force, so under totality he prevailed. Officer Davis in Ruffin v. Davis and Officer Painter in Byers v. Painter did not face an immediate deadly threat at the moment they fired, so under the same framework they lose. The Supreme Court has not abandoned officers and has not made every use of deadly force suspect. What it has done, through Barnes, the certiorari denials, and the totality framework, is require that officers be evaluated against the entire encounter.
cases.inPractice: Where the entire arc of the encounter supports the officer's perception of imminent threat, the officer wins. Where the entire arc undermines that perception, the officer loses. Felix won because the threat, a moving vehicle with him pinned beside it, was contemporaneous with his shots. The lesson for the street is to build encounters where every minute supports the officer, because the court now reviews every minute.
cases.trainIt: Use Barnes, Ruffin, and Byers together in one block. Put the three fact patterns side by side and ask trainees what the officer faced at the instant of the shot and what the officer did in the minutes before. Teach tactical patience, distance, cover, communication, and documentation as the levers that make the whole arc favor the officer. Tell command staff that the law has not moved in a hostile direction; it now looks at the whole encounter, and pre-engagement work that was sloppy under a moment-of-threat rule produces deeper civil exposure under totality.

sections.heading: Other federal circuits
sections.note: Two published Fourth Circuit opinions, both affirming the denial of qualified immunity to an officer who shot a retreating suspect, both anchored to Tennessee v. Garner. The episode covered no other circuit this week.

cases.name: Ruffin v. Davis
cases.topic: Deadly force on an armed fleeing suspect, foot pursuit, body camera review, qualified immunity
cases.caution: The episode gave no docket number and no opinion author. It did not say whether the opinion was read in full. Verify the description of the body camera analysis against the opinion before using it in training materials. A later episode in this series, October 24, 2026, corrected the May 9 description: the opinion does not announce a standalone rule about head turns, and the earlier phrasing that an officer cannot shoot because a suspect glanced backward overstated the holding.
cases.facts: In April 2020, Columbia, South Carolina was operating under a COVID curfew. Officer Kevin Davis was on patrol when he saw 17-year-old Joshua Ruffin walking through a residential neighborhood. Davis approached and identified himself, and Ruffin ran. A foot pursuit followed. At some point during the pursuit Ruffin turned his head to look back at Davis. Davis fired ten shots. One round struck Ruffin in the forehead and killed him. After the shooting, officers recovered a handgun on Ruffin's body. The gun had not been fired, and Ruffin had never pointed it at any officer. He was running away from Davis when he was hit. Davis's body camera recorded the pursuit and the shooting. Davis later said that he saw Ruffin turning his head and reasonably feared that Ruffin was about to fire. The district court denied Davis qualified immunity, and he appealed.
cases.holding: Affirmed in a published opinion issued April 29, 2026. The Fourth Circuit held that Davis was not entitled to qualified immunity, even under the specificity rule the episode calls the post-Smith rule, because the precedent that placed his conduct beyond debate was Tennessee v. Garner, decided by the Supreme Court in 1985. Under Garner, an officer may not seize an unarmed, non-dangerous suspect by shooting him dead, and even an armed suspect who is fleeing must pose an immediate threat of serious physical harm before deadly force can be used. The court rejected the argument that the gun on Ruffin's body, by itself, made the shooting reasonable. The Fourth Amendment requires armed plus an immediate threat, and the officer's perception of threat must be tied to something the suspect is doing in real time, not to what is in his pocket. Reviewing the body camera footage, the court ruled that turning one's head to face an officer is not, by itself, a movement that could reasonably be perceived as dangerous. The court did not say Davis was lying. It said that, on this record and viewing the undisputed facts in the plaintiff's favor, the head turn was not a movement that could reasonably be perceived as dangerous.
cases.notDecided: The case now goes to a jury trial, six years after the shooting. The Fourth Circuit decided only that Davis is not entitled to qualified immunity on the facts viewed at this stage; it did not decide what a jury will find about what Davis actually perceived.
cases.inPractice: The presence of a weapon on a fleeing suspect does not, standing alone, justify deadly force. Officers who shoot fleeing armed suspects without the suspect pointing the weapon, raising it, or otherwise showing an immediate threat face civil liability and may face criminal exposure. The court did not credit the officer's after-the-fact narration of what he perceived; it reviewed the footage frame by frame and reached its own conclusion about what a reasonable officer could have seen. The post-incident report does not get to rewrite what the camera shows.
cases.trainIt: Four points. First, teach deadly force authority on the Garner framework first: armed plus immediate threat is the standard, and foot pursuits should be resolved with distance, communication, containment, and resources, not with deadly force on the theory that armed equals threat. Second, teach that body camera footage is the evidentiary anchor in every deadly force case. The officer's narration on the audio matters, and the tactical decisions visible in the footage matter. Third, give foot pursuits dedicated training instead of treating them as ad hoc decisions: the geometry of the pursuit, distance from the suspect, direction of travel, what the suspect is doing with his hands, what cover and concealment exist, when to break off, and when to wait for backup or canine resources. Those decisions will be reviewed in slow motion against the totality framework. Fourth, document threat perception cleanly and contemporaneously. Verbal commands, warnings, and the threat assessment the officer voices to dispatch and to other officers in real time all become part of the record. An officer whose stated perception matches what the camera shows is in a far better position than one whose perception the video undercuts.

cases.name: Byers v. Painter
cases.decided: Late April 2026 (exact date not stated in the source)
cases.topic: Deadly force on a retreating subject in mental health crisis, continued fire after incapacitation, qualified immunity
cases.caution: The transcript spells the decedent's name both Byers and Buyers; Byers is used here because it appears more often, but confirm the caption. The episode gave no docket number, no majority author, and no exact filing date. The dissenting judge is identified only as Judge Albert Diaz.
cases.facts: In July 2023, Chesterfield County police officers contacted 34-year-old Charles Byers at his parents' home. Byers had a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder and was in mental health crisis. The encounter lasted about 90 seconds. Throughout it, Byers held a hatchet lowered at his waist. He never raised it and never made any movement suggesting he intended to use it. He was about 25 feet from the officers and was walking away from them, not toward them. He was on his parents' property and not near any bystanders. He was minimally resisting verbal commands but was not physically attacking anyone. Officer Gordon Painter fired seven shots. Five rounds struck Byers, and he died at the scene. The video showed that Painter continued firing after Byers had been hit and was further incapacitated. Painter's defense relied in part on a suicide by cop framing of the encounter. The district court denied him qualified immunity, and he appealed.
cases.holding: Affirmed in a published opinion handed down in late April 2026. The majority anchored its analysis to Tennessee v. Garner and to the totality framework the Supreme Court imposed in Barnes v. Felix. It held that it is not justifiable to use deadly force against a retreating suspect accused of a nonviolent crime who does not present an immediate danger to the officers or to others and who has already sustained multiple gunshot wounds at the hands of the police. That last clause mattered. The court treated Painter's continued fire after Byers had been hit and was further incapacitated as legally significant. The court was unsympathetic to the suicide by cop framing. A subject who is walking away from the officers, holding the weapon at his waist and not moving aggressively, is not presenting a suicide by cop fact pattern. He is a retreating subject in mental health crisis. The denial of qualified immunity was upheld, so the claim against Painter goes forward.
cases.dissent: Judge Albert Diaz dissented. In his view, Painter's actions did not violate clearly established law. The episode read the dissent as reflecting the genuine doctrinal difficulty of behavioral health cases under the post-Smith specificity rule, but the majority controls.
cases.inPractice: A subject with an edged weapon held at his waist, 25 feet away and walking away from officers, is a subject for positioning, communication, and resource staging, not engagement. Continued fire after the subject has been hit and is incapacitated is its own legally significant act. And a suicide by cop defense does not survive a retreating subject; the behavioral cues of a retreating person in crisis are different, and so is the legal exposure.
cases.trainIt: Three points for the behavioral health crisis posture. First, time, distance, and cover are doctrine, not preference. Ninety seconds is not enough time to manage a behavioral health crisis, and 25 feet is communicate distance, not closing distance. Slow the encounter down. Second, CIT training is now backed by appellate review. The episode read Byers as effectively elevating crisis intervention principles to the constitutional baseline for behavioral health calls. Train officers in CIT, train supervisors to recognize behavioral health indicators on dispatch, and train dispatch staff to flag known behavioral health subjects so responding officers know what they are walking into. Agencies that have built that infrastructure will fare better in litigation. Third, train officers to read the difference between a suicide by cop fact pattern and a retreating subject in crisis. The cues are different, the training response is different, and the legal exposure is different.

applications.title: Armed alone is not enough
applications.body: A weapon on a fleeing suspect does not by itself satisfy Garner. The standard is armed plus immediate threat, tied to something the suspect is doing in real time. Train deadly force authority on the Garner framework first, and treat the specificity rule as no shield when the controlling precedent is a Supreme Court holding squarely on point.

applications.title: The camera is the record
applications.body: In Ruffin the court reviewed the footage frame by frame rather than crediting the officer's after-the-fact account. Teach officers to narrate commands, warnings, and threat perception out loud and in real time, so the record matches what the camera shows.

applications.title: Give foot pursuits their own training block
applications.body: Most agencies train traffic stops in detail and leave foot pursuits to improvisation. Teach distance, direction of travel, the suspect's hands, cover and concealment, when to break off, and when to wait for backup or a canine. Those choices will be replayed in slow motion.

applications.title: Crisis calls run on a different cadence
applications.body: Twenty-five feet is communicate distance, not closing distance, and 90 seconds is not enough time to manage a crisis. Slow it down, use distance and cover, and stage CIT-trained resources. Flag known behavioral health subjects at dispatch so officers know what they are walking into.

applications.title: Every round after incapacitation is its own decision
applications.body: The Byers court treated continued fire after the subject had been hit and was further incapacitated as legally significant. Train officers to reassess after each shot and to stop when the threat stops.

applications.title: The totality framework cuts both ways
applications.body: Felix won because the threat was contemporaneous with his shots. Davis and Painter lost because it was not. Build encounters where the whole arc supports the officer: tactical patience, distance, cover, communication, and documentation are the levers.

quiz.q: In Ruffin v. Davis, why did the handgun recovered from Ruffin's body not make the shooting reasonable?
options: Because the gun was not loaded
Because an armed fleeing suspect must also pose an immediate threat, and turning to look back is not a movement that could reasonably be perceived as dangerous
Because the officer never saw the gun
Because the curfew made the stop unlawful
quiz.teach: Under Tennessee v. Garner, armed alone is not enough. The Fourth Amendment requires armed plus an immediate threat tied to what the suspect is doing in real time, and the court reached that conclusion from the body camera footage rather than the officer's later account.

quiz.q: What fact did the Byers v. Painter majority treat as legally significant beyond the initial decision to fire?
options: That Byers was on private property
That the officer had CIT training
That the officer continued firing after Byers had been hit and was further incapacitated
That the hatchet was later found to be dull
quiz.teach: The court held that deadly force is not justified against a retreating, nonviolent subject who poses no immediate danger and who has already sustained multiple gunshot wounds. Each round after incapacitation is its own decision.

quiz.q: What was the effect of the Supreme Court's April 27, 2026 action in Barnes v. Felix?
options: It reversed the Fifth Circuit and sent the case to trial
It denied certiorari for the second time, leaving the Fifth Circuit's qualified immunity ruling for Deputy Constable Felix final
It granted review of the totality framework
quiz.teach: Felix prevailed under the totality framework because the threat, a moving vehicle with him hemmed in beside it, was contemporaneous with his use of force. The same framework produced losses for the officers in Ruffin and Byers, where the suspects were retreating.
